summary: Defines optional extensions to the Simple Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (STAMP) that allow measuring additional performance metrics. It also defines a STAMP Test Session Identifier, and updates RFC 8762.

eli5.summary: STAMP is a way to time how long messages take to travel across a network. This adds extra measurements and a way to label each test.

questions: how to measure network performance with stamp
what is the stamp session identifier
what tlv types does stamp define
how does the stamp hmac tlv work
subtitle: Optional add-on fields that let STAMP test packets carry location, timing, class-of-service and integrity data.

tldr.problem: The base Simple Two-way Active Measurement Protocol (STAMP) measures delay and loss with fixed-format test packets, and gives no room to ask a reflector for extra information or to protect that information.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8972 appends optional Type-Length-Value (TLV) elements after the base packet: padding, location, timestamp information, class of service, direct counters, access reports, follow-up timestamps and an HMAC. It also adds a 2-octet Session Identifier to the base packet.
tldr.outcome: Senders can request richer measurements from reflectors that understand the TLVs, while reflectors that do not simply mark the TLVs as unrecognized. The document updates RFC 8762.

today: RFC 8972 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 8762. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the Extensions Add
sections.content:
The Simple Two-way Active Measurement Protocol (STAMP, RFC 8762) defines the base functions: a Session-Sender sends test packets to a Session-Reflector, which sends them back so that delay, latency, packet loss, duplication and out-of-order delivery can be measured.

RFC 8972 specifies optional extensions that use Type-Length-Value (TLV) encoding, describes their formats and how they operate, and defines a STAMP Test Session Identifier as an update of the base specification.
sections.eli5: STAMP is a game of catch used to time a network. This document adds optional sticky notes you can attach to the ball to ask extra questions.

sections.title: The STAMP Session Identifier
sections.content:
A STAMP session is normally identified by a 4-tuple: source and destination IP addresses and source and destination UDP port numbers. A Session-Sender MAY add a locally unique STAMP Session Identifier (SSID), a two-octet, non-zero unsigned integer. How it is generated is implementation specific, but an implementation MUST NOT give the same identifier to different test sessions. If the SSID is used, it MUST be present in every test packet of that session.

A Session-Reflector that supports the specification MUST identify a session using the SSID together with elements of the usual 4-tuple, and MUST be provisioned with those elements before the session starts. It MUST discard non-matching test packets and MUST copy the SSID from the received packet into the reflected one.

A reflector that does not support the specification returns a zeroed SSID. The Session-Sender MAY then stop the session, and an implementation MUST let the operator control this behavior. Otherwise it can, for example, fall back to sending base STAMP packets.
sections.eli5: The session number is like a name tag on your ball. The other player copies the tag back, so you know the ball you got is the one you threw.

sections.title: How TLVs Are Added to Packets
sections.content:
TLVs are an optional field after the base STAMP test packet, and several MAY appear in one packet. Each TLV has a one-octet STAMP TLV Flags field, a one-octet Type field and a two-octet Length field equal to the length of the Value in octets. Multi-byte fields are in network byte order. A node tells whether a packet carries TLVs by comparing the UDP Length with the length of the base packet for the configured mode.

Three flags are defined. U (Unrecognized) is set to 1 by the sender; the reflector sets it to 1 if it did not understand the TLV and to 0 otherwise. M (Malformed) is set by a reflector when the Length is not valid for the type or the TLV does not fit in the packet. I (Integrity) is set by a reflector when the extensions fail HMAC verification. Five reserved bits MUST be zero on transmit and ignored on receipt.

A reflector that does not recognize a Type MUST copy the TLV unchanged, set U to 1 and skip it. When a sender sees U it skips that TLV, on M it stops processing the rest of the packet, and on I it discards all TLVs and stops. Types in the Private Use range must carry the vendor's SMI Private Enterprise Code in the first four octets of the Value.
sections.eli5: Each sticky note has a small label saying what kind it is and how long it is. If the other player cannot read a note, they stick it back on the ball marked 'did not understand'.

sections.title: The Defined TLVs
sections.content:
Extra Padding (type 1) makes test packets larger than the base packet, which is 44 octets in unauthenticated mode and 112 octets in authenticated mode. It SHOULD be filled with pseudorandom numbers and can appear more than once.

Location (type 2) lets the sender ask the reflector for the source MAC address, destination IP address and source IP address it saw, using sub-TLVs. The reflector answers with the specific EUI-48, EUI-64, IPv4 or IPv6 forms. The text says this can reveal a path switch on the last hop and the presence of a NAT router.

Timestamp Information (type 3) reports the clock synchronization source (for example NTP or PTP) and the timestamping method used at the reflector's ingress and egress. Class of Service (type 4) carries DSCP1 (the DSCP the sender wants on the reflected packet), DSCP2 and ECN (what the reflector received) and a two-bit Reverse Path flag RP. If local policy does not permit the requested DSCP, the reflector uses the received DSCP and sets RP to 1, so only the forward direction can be analyzed.

Direct Measurement (type 5) carries counters of in-profile packets: S_TxC, R_RxC and R_TxC, four octets each. Access Report (type 6) lets a sender signal access network status, with an Access ID of 1 (3GPP) or 2 (non-3GPP) and a return code. The sender arms a retransmission timer, with a default of three seconds, and retransmits up to four times. Follow-Up Telemetry (type 7) lets a reflector report, in a later packet, a better timestamp for an earlier reflected packet.
sections.eli5: Each kind of note asks a different question: how big was the ball, where did it come from, which clock was used, what lane was it in, and how many balls were counted.

sections.title: Protecting TLVs with the HMAC TLV
sections.content:
The HMAC TLV (type 8) has a 16-octet HMAC field. As in RFC 8762, STAMP uses HMAC-SHA-256 truncated to 128 bits. The HMAC is computed over the Sequence Number field of the base packet concatenated with all preceding TLVs.

Authenticated-mode packets MUST include the HMAC TLV, unless the only TLV present is the Extra Padding TLV. It MUST follow all other TLVs. In unauthenticated mode it MAY be used, and implementations MUST provide controls to enable it. The HMAC MUST be verified before using data in the TLVs.

If a reflector's verification fails, it stops processing, copies the TLVs into the reflected packet and sets the I flag to 1 in each. A sender that sees I set, or whose own verification fails, stops processing TLVs. Key management is out of scope.
sections.eli5: The HMAC is a secret seal on the sticky notes. If the seal does not match, the notes cannot be trusted and are ignored.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
IANA created six subregistries under the STAMP registry: TLV Types, TLV Flags, Sub-TLV Types, Synchronization Sources, Timestamping Methods and Return Codes. TLV Types 1 to 175 are allocated by IETF Review, 176 to 239 First Come First Served, 240 to 251 are for Experimental Use and 252 to 254 for Private Use. Values 0 and 255 are reserved.

Synchronization sources include NTP (1), PTP (2), SSU/BITS (3), GPS/GLONASS/LORAN-C/BDS/Galileo (4) and local free-running (5). Timestamping methods are HW Assist (1), SW Local (2) and Control Plane (3). Return codes are Network available (1) and Network unavailable (2).
sections.eli5: IANA keeps the official list of note types and codes, so everyone uses the same numbers for the same meaning.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extensions inherit the security considerations of the base protocol. The HMAC TLV protects the integrity of the extensions, but the RFC states that it does not protect against a replay attack.

To guard against malformed TLVs, senders and reflectors MUST check the M flag and validate the Length field. Because the Class of Service TLV can test DSCP mapping, the document also inherits the considerations of RFC 2474. Since sender and reflector may sit in domains with different CoS profiles, operators should verify the CoS values used in the reflector's domain, and a reflector SHOULD support a local policy to confirm whether the requested DSCP may be used.
sections.eli5: The seal stops people changing the notes, but it cannot stop someone from re-sending an old ball. Players should also check that each note makes sense before acting on it.

fields.name: STAMP TLV Flags
fields.desc: U, M and I flags plus five reserved bits.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Allocated by IANA; says how to read the Value.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the Value field in octets.

items.label: Extra Padding
items.desc: Makes test packets larger than the base packet.

items.label: Location
items.desc: Asks the reflector for MAC and IP address information.

items.label: Timestamp Information
items.desc: Clock synchronization source and timestamp method.

items.label: Class of Service
items.desc: DSCP and ECN information and reverse-path flag.

items.label: Access Report
items.desc: Access network status, retransmitted until reflected.

items.label: Follow-Up Telemetry
items.desc: A later, better timestamp for a reflected packet.

items.label: HMAC
items.desc: Integrity check over the preceding TLVs.
